metadata.title: Two Resolutions, One Click — The macOS Coordinate Roundtrip.
metadata.purpose: Answer one real question in the Plain register: Claude's click coordinates come back in the space of a resized screenshot — how do you get that click to land on your Mac's real, native display? Lands the carry-out that Claude's click lives in the resized copy, and the original-over-sent ratio is what maps it back.
metadata.anchor_pair: B02 -> B04 (native screen 1920x1080, button at 960,540; resized to 1456x819 the button reads 728,409; inverted back it lands at 960,540 exactly)

beats.narration_text: Someone assumes a Retina screenshot reaches Claude at native resolution. It doesn't — the API resizes it first, into a canvas you never saw. So how do you get Claude's click back onto your real screen?

beats.narration_text: Retina displays put screenshots well over Claude's vision budget: the encoder tiles every image into 28-by-28 patches, capped at 1568 pixels on the long edge and 1568 tiles total. One input pipeline, not one per screen resolution — that's the design choice, and the cost is that every coordinate Claude reports lives in the resized canvas, not yours. Send the raw click straight through and the server resizes anyway, in a space you never got to inspect.

shot.new_visual_element: A large native-screenshot rectangle far exceeding a capped tile grid; the same raw coordinate carried straight across into the grid and missing

production_viz.label: Over budget, resized either way
production_viz.mechanic: Left: a large outlined rectangle labelled 'NATIVE RETINA SCREENSHOT' on cream, visibly oversized. Right: a smaller tile-grid rectangle labelled '≤1568px long edge, ≤1568 tiles'. An arrow carries a raw (x,y) dot straight across unscaled; on the tile grid the dot lands off a target ring, marked with a cross.

beats.narration_text: Here's the concrete case. Your screen is 1920 by 1080, and the button sits at 960, 540 — dead center. Before Claude ever looks, the reference implementation's target underscore image underscore size shrinks the screenshot to 1456 by 819. Same physical button, but on that resized image it now sits at 728, 409. Two different numbers for the same pixel — the direct consequence of the encoder having one canvas and your Mac having another.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR - native rect 1920x1080 with a dot at (960,540); resized rect 1456x819 with the same button now plotted at (728,409)

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR - one button, two numbers
production_viz.mechanic: THE ANCHOR. Left rectangle labelled '1920 × 1080 — native' with a terracotta dot dead center, captioned '(960, 540)'. Right rectangle labelled '1456 × 819 — sent to Claude' (visibly smaller, same aspect). An arrow from left to right carries the SAME physical button; on the right rectangle it's captioned '(728, 409)'. THIS EXACT PAIR OF RECTANGLES RETURNS AT B04.

beats.narration_text: Here's what target underscore image underscore size is actually doing: a binary search for the largest width and height that keep the long edge under 1568 pixels, keep the tile count under 1568, and preserve the aspect ratio. You call it yourself before you ever send the screenshot, and you record what it returns — 1456 by 819. Those sent dimensions are the denominator of every inverse you'll ever compute. Skip recording them and the math has nothing to divide by.

shot.new_visual_element: Algorithm card: binary search over (w,h) under the long-edge and tile-count caps, resolving to (1456, 819); a note to record sent_w, sent_h

production_viz.label: The forward call
production_viz.mechanic: Two lines build in ink mono on cream: 'target_image_size(1920, 1080)' then an arrow down to '→ (1456, 819)'. Beneath, a smaller line in terracotta: 'record sent_w, sent_h — the denominator of the inverse'. A small caption bottom-right: 'image.py — binary search, long-edge ≤1568, tiles ≤1568'.

beats.narration_text: Now invert it. Real equals model coordinate times original over sent — you're just undoing the shrink, one axis at a time. 728 times 1920 over 1456 is 960. 409 times 1080 over 819 is 540 — the click lands exactly on the button. That inverse only works because you kept the sent dimensions from your own call. Skip that step, or hand it a screenshot already inside the tile budget, and target underscore image underscore size returns the input unchanged — there's nothing to invert. That's the caveat, not the main case.

shot.new_visual_element: THE ANCHOR RETURNS - same two rectangles; the (728,409) dot carried back by the ratio lands exactly on the (960,540) button; a third already-in-budget rectangle passes through unchanged, struck through

production_viz.label: THE ANCHOR RETURNS - inverted, and it lands
production_viz.mechanic: THE B02 RECTANGLE PAIR RETURNS, identical. This time the (728, 409) dot on the small rectangle is carried back across with the ratio applied, landing exactly on the button at '(960, 540)' inside the 1920×1080 rectangle, marked with a check. Off to the side, a third rectangle already within the tile budget passes straight through with a dashed 'unchanged' arrow, captioned 'nothing to invert' in ink — the caveat, not the main case.

beats.narration_text: On macOS, Claude's click lands in the resized copy of your screenshot, not your native display — record what target underscore image underscore size returned, then multiply by original over sent to get back to a real pixel.

props.quote: Claude's click lands in the resized copy of your screenshot, not your native display — record what target_image_size returned, then multiply by original over sent to get back to a real pixel.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's the prompt — read it with me. I'm on macOS with a Retina display. Before Claude sees my screenshot, target_image_size resizes it — 1920 by 1080 becomes 1456 by 819. Write me a Python function that takes Claude's reported (x, y), the original screen size, and the sent size, and returns the real pixel, clamped to the display. Then go deeper: what does target_image_size return when the screenshot is already inside the 1568-pixel and 1568-tile budget — does the inverse become a no-op, or a wrong divide waiting to bite? Liam, in for Bear.

llm_exercise.prompt: I'm on macOS with a Retina display, calling Anthropic's computer-use API. Before Claude sees my screenshot, the reference implementation's target_image_size resizes it to fit a 1568-pixel long-edge and 1568-tile budget — for example, 1920×1080 becomes 1456×819. Write me a Python function that takes Claude's reported (x, y), the original screen size (orig_w, orig_h), and the actual sent size (sent_w, sent_h), and returns the real-screen click coordinate, clamped to the display. Explain each line, and note why recording sent_w and sent_h before the API call is required — not optional.
llm_exercise.dig_deeper: Go deeper: what does target_image_size return when the screenshot is already inside the 1568-pixel long-edge and 1568-tile budget — does it pass the dimensions through unchanged? If so, what should your inverse do when orig == sent, and how could a naive caller silently multiply by 1.0 and never notice the resize never happened?
